verses.zh: 当以色列中没有王的时候，有住以法莲山地那边的一个利未人，娶了一个犹大伯利恒的女子为妾。
verses.en: In those days Israel had no king. There was a Levite[NOTE:1] living temporarily in the remote region of the Ephraimite hill country. He acquired a concubine[NOTE:2] from Bethlehem[NOTE:3] in Judah.
notes: Heb “a man, a Levite.”
See the note on the word “concubine” in 8:31.
For location see Map5-B1; Map7-E2; Map8-E2; Map10-B4.
verses.commentary:
19:1 "in those days" Though this idiom is not specific, it is a textual marker for a later editor/compiler. Judges
was written during the United Monarchy (i.e., Saul and David). See note at Jdgs. 17:6.

▣ "concubine" This was a second level, legal wife whose children had no inheritance rights.

verses.zh: 妾行淫离开丈夫，回犹大的伯利恒，到了父家，在那里住了四个月。
verses.en: However, she[NOTE:1] got angry at him[NOTE:2] and went home[NOTE:3] to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah. When she had been there four months,
notes: Heb “and his concubine.” The pronoun (“she”) has been used in the translation for stylistic reasons.

Or “was unfaithful to him.” Many have understood the Hebrew verb וַתִּזְנֶה (vattizneh) as being from זָנָה (zanah, “to be a prostitute”), but it may be derived from a root meaning “to be angry; to hate” attested in Akkadian (see HALOT 275 s.v. II זנה).
Heb “went from him.”
verses.commentary:
19:2 "played the harlot against him" This is the reading of the MT and Peshitta, but the Vulgate has "she
was angry and left him." The LXXA has "became angry with him," like the Vulgate, but LXXB
has "left him." It seems that the context supports the MT, if understood in the sense of the Vulgate. For a wife to
leave her husband was not allowed. When she left, everyone would assume she had committed an unfaithful act and
was put away by her husband (cf. Matt. 19:9; Mark 10:11-12).

The UBS Text Project, p. 120, says there were three meanings for the VERB (BDB 275, KB 278).

- play the harlot ‒ זנה I, KB 275

- became angry with ‒ זנה II, KB 275 (Akkadiana root)

- go away

In this context, #2 fits best.

verses.zh: 她丈夫起来，带着一个仆人、两匹驴去见她，用好话劝她回来。女子就引丈夫进入父家。她父见了那人，便欢欢喜喜地迎接。
verses.en: her husband came[NOTE:1] after her, hoping he could convince her to return.[NOTE:2] He brought with him his servant[NOTE:3] and a pair of donkeys. When she brought him into her father’s house and the girl’s father saw him, he greeted him warmly.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “arose and came.”
Heb “to speak to her heart to bring her back.”
Or “young man.”
Heb “he was happy to meet him.”
verses.commentary:
19:3

NASB, NRSV
"to speak tenderly to her"

NKJV
"to speak kindly to her"

NJB
"to appeal to her affections"

JPSOA
"to woo. . .to win her back"

REB
"to appeal to her"

LXX
"to speak to her heart"

Peshitta
"to speak lovingly to her"

The MT is literally "to speak to her heart" (BDB 524). This is an idiom for "wooing" or "courting"
(i.e., intimate love conversations, cf. Gen. 34:3; Ruth 2:13).

▣ "his servant and a pair of donkeys" In the culture of the day these donkeys would have carried a gift
for the father of the concubine. This apparently was a wealthy Levite.

It is also possible that these donkeys were merely transportation for

- the concubine to return home

- provisions for the trip (Jdgs. 19:19)

- a ride for the Levite

verses.zh: 那人的岳父，就是女子的父亲，将那人留下住了三天。于是二人一同吃喝、住宿。
verses.en: His father-in-law, the girl’s father, persuaded him to stay with him for three days, and they ate and drank together, and spent the night there.
verses.commentary:
19:4-9 This describes the father-in-law's joy and hospitality over the reunion and gift from the Levite. It
includes many IMPERATIVES OF REQUEST.

Jdgs. 19:5 ‒ "sustain yourself with a piece of bread" ‒ Qal MPERATIVE

Jdgs. 19:6

- "please be willing to spend the night" ‒ Hiphil MPERATIVE and Qal IMPERATIVE;
this VERB (BDB 533, KB 529) is used eleven times in this chapter

- Same as 1.

- "let your heart be merry" ‒ Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

Jdgs. 19:8

- "please sustain yourself" ‒ like Jdgs. 19:5

- "wait" ‒ Hithpael IMPERATIVE

Jdgs. 19:9

- "please spend the night" ‒ like 19:6, #1

- "spend the night" (twice) ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE, like 19:6, #1 and 19:9, #1

- "that your heart be merry" ‒ like 19:6, #3

verses.zh: 到第四天，利未人清早起来要走，女子的父亲对女婿说：「请你吃点饭，加添心力，然后可以行路。」
verses.en: On the fourth day they woke up early and the Levite got ready to leave.[NOTE:1] But the girl’s father said to his son-in-law, “Have a bite to eat for some energy,[NOTE:2] then you can go.”
notes: Heb “and he arose to go.”
Heb “Sustain your heart [with] a bit of food.”

verses.zh: 于是二人坐下一同吃喝。女子的父亲对那人说：「请你再住一夜，畅快你的心。」
verses.en: So the two of them sat down and had a meal together.[NOTE:1] Then the girl’s father said to the man, “Why not stay another night and have a good time?”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “And they sat and ate, the two of them together, and they drank.”
Heb “Be willing and spend the night so that your heart might be good.”

verses.zh: 那人起来要走，他岳父强留他，他又住了一宿。
verses.en: When the man got ready to leave,[NOTE:1] his father-in-law convinced him to stay another night.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and the man arose to go.”
Heb “his father-in-law persuaded him and he again spent the night there.”

verses.zh: 到第五天，他清早起来要走，女子的父亲说：「请你吃点饭，加添心力，等到日头偏西再走。」于是二人一同吃饭。
verses.en: He woke up early in the morning on the fifth day so he could leave, but the girl’s father said, “Get some energy![NOTE:1] Wait until later in the day to leave.”[NOTE:2] So they ate a meal together.
notes: Heb “Sustain your heart.” He is once more inviting him to stay for a meal.
Heb “Wait until the declining of the day.”

verses.zh: 那人同他的妾和仆人起来要走，他岳父，就是女子的父亲，对他说：「看哪，日头偏西了，请你再住一夜；天快晚了，可以在这里住宿，畅快你的心。明天早早起行回家去。」
verses.en: When the man got ready to leave[NOTE:1] with his concubine and his servant,[NOTE:2] his father-in-law, the girl’s father, said to him, “Look! The day is almost over.[NOTE:3] Stay another night! Since the day is over,[NOTE:4] stay another night here and have a good time. You can get up early tomorrow and start your trip home.”[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “the man arose to go.”
Or “young man.”
Heb “the day is sinking to become evening.”
Or “declining.”
Heb “for your way and go to your tent.”

verses.zh: 那人不愿再住一夜，就备上那两匹驴，带着妾起身走了，来到耶布斯的对面（耶布斯就是耶路撒冷。）
verses.en: But the man did not want to stay another night. He left[NOTE:1] and traveled as far as[NOTE:2] Jebus (that is, Jerusalem).[NOTE:3] He had with him a pair of saddled donkeys and his concubine.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “and he arose and went.”
Heb “to the front of.”
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Some ancient witnesses add “and his servant.”
verses.commentary:
19:10 "Jebus (that is, Jerusalem)" The city was first called Salem (cf. Gen. 14:18). Later it was called
Jebus after its inhabitants, the Jebusites, origin unknown. Finally, it was called Jerusalem, possibly after David
made it his capital (cf. 2 Sam. 5:6-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: MORIAH, SALEM, JEBUS, ZION, JERUSALEM

verses.zh: 临近耶布斯的时候，日头快要落了，仆人对主人说：「我们不如进这耶布斯人的城里住宿。」
verses.en: When they got near Jebus, it was getting quite late[NOTE:1] and the servant[NOTE:2] said to his master, “Come on, let’s stop at[NOTE:3] this Jebusite city and spend the night in it.”
notes: Heb “and the day was descending greatly.”
Or “young man.”
Heb “turn aside” (also in the following verse).
verses.commentary:
19:11-13 The servant requests that they stay in Jebus.

- "please come" ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE

- "let us turn aside" ‒ Qal COHORTATIVE

- "spend the night" ‒ Qal IMPERFECT used in a COHORTATIVE sense

But the Levite did not want to stay in a Canaanite city (Jdgs. 19:12, irony). So, they moved on.

- "come" ‒ Qal IMPERATIVE, like Jdgs. 19:11, #1

- "let us approach. . ." ‒ Qal COHORTATIVE

The servant requested but the Levite commanded.

verses.zh: 主人回答说：「我们不可进不是以色列人住的外邦城，不如过到基比亚去」；
verses.en: But his master said to him, “We should not stop at a foreign city where non-Israelites live.[NOTE:1] We will travel on to Gibeah.”
notes: Heb “[in] which not any of the sons of Israel [are] here.”

verses.zh: 又对仆人说：「我们可以到一个地方，或住在基比亚，或住在拉玛。」
verses.en: He said to his servant,[NOTE:1] “Come on, we will go into one of the other towns[NOTE:2] and spend the night in Gibeah or Ramah.”
notes: Or “young man.”
Heb “we will enter one of the places.”
verses.commentary:
19:13 "Gibeah" The town was 4 miles north of Jerusalem. It was Saul's birthplace and capital (cf. 1 Sam.
10:26; 11:4; 15:34). However, because of robbers, one could not travel at night. There may be a purposeful
comparison of the cities associated with Saul (i.e., Gibeah) and the cities associated with David (Bethlehem,
Jebus, Ramah). Remember, Judges was written during the United Monarchy (i.e., Saul then David).

There are three Gibeahs.

- in Judah ‒ Joshua 15:20, 57

- in Ephraim ‒ Joshua 24:33

- Saul's capital ‒ Jdgs. 20:31; 2 Sam. 10:26; 11:4

▣ "Ramah" Ramah was 2 miles farther. It was the hometown of Samuel.

verses.zh: 他们就往前走。将到便雅悯的基比亚，日头已经落了；
verses.en: So they traveled on,[NOTE:1] and the sun went down when they were near Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and they passed by and went.”
Heb “which belongs to Benjamin.”

verses.zh: 他们进入基比亚要在那里住宿，就坐在城里的街上，因为无人接他们进家住宿。
verses.en: They stopped there and decided to spend the night[NOTE:1] in Gibeah. They came into the city and sat down in the town square, but no one invited them to spend the night.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “they turned aside there to enter to spend the night.”
Heb “and he entered and sat down, and there was no one receiving them into the house to spend the night.”
verses.commentary:
19:15 "they sat down in the open square of the city, for no one took them into his house" This was a
shameful act of the citizens not offering hospitality, which was so important in that day.

verses.zh: 晚上，有一个老年人从田间做工回来。他原是以法莲山地的人，住在基比亚；那地方的人却是便雅悯人。
verses.en: But then an old man passed by, returning at the end of the day from his work in the field.[NOTE:1] The man was from the Ephraimite hill country; he was living temporarily in Gibeah. (The residents of the town were Benjaminites.)[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “And look, an old man was coming from his work, from the field in the evening.”
Heb “And the men of the place were Benjaminites.”
verses.commentary: 19:16 "the man was from the hill country of Ephraim" This is the same area that the Levite was from.

verses.zh: 老年人举目看见客人坐在城里的街上，就问他说：「你从哪里来？要往哪里去？」
verses.en: When he looked up and saw the traveler[NOTE:1] in the town square, the old man said, “Where are you heading? Where do you come from?”
notes: Heb “the man, the traveler.”

verses.zh: 他回答说：「我们从犹大的伯利恒来，要往以法莲山地那边去。我原是那里的人，到过犹大的伯利恒，现在我往耶和华的殿去，在这里无人接我进他的家。
verses.en: The Levite[NOTE:1] said to him, “We are traveling from Bethlehem[NOTE:2] in Judah to the remote region of the Ephraimite hill country. That’s where I’m from. I had business in Bethlehem in Judah, but now I’m heading home.[NOTE:3] But no one has invited me into their home.
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (the Levite) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
For location see Map5-B1; Map7-E2; Map8-E2; Map10-B4.
Heb “I went to Bethlehem in Judah, but [to] the house of the Lord I am going.” The Hebrew text has “house of the Lord,” which might refer to the shrine at Shiloh. The LXX reads “to my house.”
verses.commentary:
19:18

NASB, NRSV
"to my house"

NKJV, JPSOA, Peshitta
"to the house of the Lord"

TEV
"to our home"

NJB, REB, LXX
"I am going home"

The MT has "to the house of YHWH," but the LXX has "to my home." The difference between "my"
(LXX) and "YHWH" (MT) is very close in Hebrew. Possibly the final yod (י) was
mistakenly made the first letter (aberration) of the divine name,
יהוה, by later Hebrew scribes.

Since the VERB "cut" in Jdgs. 19:29 has sacrificial connotations, some think the Levite
dismembered his concubine at the shrine at Shiloh (cf. Jos. 18:1; Jdgs. 18:31) or even at Bethel (cf. Jdgs. 20:26-28) in a
ritual manner.

verses.zh: 其实我有粮草可以喂驴，我与我的妾，并我的仆人，有饼有酒，并不缺少甚么。」
verses.en: We have enough straw and grain for our donkeys, and there is enough food and wine for me, your female servant,[NOTE:1] and the young man who is with your servants.[NOTE:2] We lack nothing.”
notes: By calling his concubine the old man’s “female servant,” the Levite emphasizes their dependence on him for shelter.

Some Hebrew mss and ancient witnesses read the singular, “your servant,” which would refer to the Levite. If one retains the plural, then both the Levite and his wife are in view. In either case the pronominal suffix emphasizes their dependence on the old man for shelter.
verses.commentary:
19:19 The Levite is clearly stating he brought all the provisions for his trip. He needs no assistance of any
kind, except a place to stay (i.e., house). The lavish hospitality of his concubine's father is not expected.

However, the culture demanded the host provide the needs and protection of guests (BDB 533, KB
529, Qal JUSSIVE, Jdgs. 19:20, cf. 19:21).

- washed their feet, cf. Gen. 18:4; 24:32; 43:24

- provided food

- provided drink

- provided a place to sleep

- tended to their animals

It was not as elaborate as the concubine's father, but still very expensive for this poor farmer and his
unmarried daughter.

▣ "your servants" The MT (LXXB) has the PLURAL but the context
demands the SINGULAR (Targum, Peshitta, Vulgate). The JPSOA footnote implies the
PLURAL reflects:

- the concubine

- the servant

- the host and his daughter also called "your servants" (i.e., Oriental eastern hospitality)

- Same as 3.

▣ "they washed their feet and ate and drank" This is normal etiquette. The "they" may refer to the
Levite's servant or the man and his daughter.

verses.zh: 老年人说：「愿你平安！你所需用的我都给你，只是不可在街上过夜。」
verses.en: The old man said, “Everything is just fine.[NOTE:1] I will take care of all your needs. But don’t spend the night in the town square.”
notes: Heb “Peace to you.”

verses.zh: 于是领他们到家里，喂上驴，他们就洗脚吃喝。
verses.en: So he brought him to his house and fed the donkeys. They washed their feet and had a meal.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “ate and drank.”

verses.zh: 他们心里正欢畅的时候，城中的匪徒围住房子，连连叩门，对房主老人说：「你把那进你家的人带出来，我们要与他交合。」
verses.en: They were having a good time,[NOTE:1] when suddenly[NOTE:2] some men of the city, some good-for-nothings,[NOTE:3] surrounded the house and kept beating[NOTE:4] on the door. They said to the old man who owned the house, “Send out the man who came to visit you so we can take carnal knowledge of him.”[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “they were making their heart good.”
Heb “and look.”

Heb “the men of the city, men, the sons of wickedness.” The phrases are in apposition; the last phrase specifies what type of men they were. It is not certain if all the men of the city are in view, or just a group of troublemakers. In 20:5 the town leaders are implicated in the crime, suggesting that all the men of the city were involved. If so, the implication is that the entire male population of the town were good-for-nothings.
The Hitpael verb form appears to have an iterative force here, indicating repeated action.

Heb “know.” The expression יָדַע (yadaʿ) “to know” is a euphemism for sexual relations. Elsewhere NET employs the English euphemism “be intimate with” for this use of יָדַע (yadaʿ), but uses a different euphemism here because of the perverse overtones of force in this context. Their intent is to molest him, but their rhetoric tries to minimize their wickedness.
verses.commentary:
19:22 "worthless fellows" This is literally "sons of Belial," from two Hebrew words, "sons of worthlessness"
(BDB 116, cf. Deut. 13:13; 1 Sam. 2:12). Later, in the Apocrypha it became a title for Satan (cf. 2 Cor. 6:15).

▣ "that we may have sexual relations with him" This aggressive homosexuality reminds one of Sodom
(cf. Genesis 19). These Israelites were acting like perverse Canaanites. Homosexuality was a way to highlight the evil
of the day (cf. Rom. 1:26,27, and also note NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 1209, #8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HOMOSEXUALITY

verses.zh: 那房主出来对他们说：「弟兄们哪，不要这样作恶；这人既然进了我的家，你们就不要行这丑事。
verses.en: The man who owned the house went outside and said to them, “No, my brothers! Don’t do this wicked thing! After all, this man is a guest in my house. Don’t do such a disgraceful thing!
verses.commentary:
19:23-24 This shows the cultural importance attached to ANE hospitality.

19:23 Notice how this request is characterized.

- "do not act so wickedly" ‒ BDB 949, KB 1269, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a
JUSSIVE sense, cf. Gen. 19:7

- "do not commit this act of folly" ‒ BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERFECT used in a
JUSSIVE sense; the NOUN "folly" (BDB 615) means "senseless" or "disgraceful,"
cf. Gen. 34:7; Deut. 22:21; Jos. 7:15; 2 Sam. 13:12; Jer. 29:33; it usually has a sexual connotation

There is no NEGATIVE IMPERATIVE, so Hebrew expresses this with a
NEGATIVE and a JUSSIVE (cf. Gen. 13:8).

verses.zh: 我有个女儿，还是处女，并有这人的妾，我将她们领出来任凭你们玷辱她们，只是向这人不可行这样的丑事。」
verses.en: Here are my virgin daughter and my guest’s[NOTE:1] concubine. I will send them out, and you can abuse them and do to them whatever you like.[NOTE:2] But don’t do such a disgraceful thing to this man!”
notes: Heb “his”; the referent (the visiting Levite) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “what is good in your eyes.”
verses.commentary:
19:24 This shows the low morality and place of women in that day. Notice the IMPERATIVES.

The man offers both his virgin (BDB 143) daughter and the Levite's concubine.

- "to ravish them" ‒ BDB 776, KB 853, Qal IMPERATIVE, which means to humble a woman by
sexual relations, cf. Gen. 34:2; Deut. 21:14; 22:24, 29; Jdgs. 20:5; 2 Sam. 13:12, 14, 22, 32; Lam. 5:11; Ezek. 22:10, 11

- "do to them whatever you wish" ‒ BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE

This incident is so shocking. One wonders if the man thought that since the crowd wanted to have sex with
the Levite, maybe they would not want to have sex with a woman.

At any rate, this shows clearly

- the gracious and absolute requirement of ANE hospitality

- the cowardly act of these men to save their own lives

- the terrible plight of women in the ANE (i.e., property)

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

verses.zh: 那些人却不听从他的话。那人就把他的妾拉出去交给他们，他们便与她交合，终夜凌辱她，直到天色快亮才放她去。
verses.en: The men refused to listen to him, so the Levite[NOTE:1] grabbed his concubine and made her go outside.[NOTE:2] They raped[NOTE:3] her and abused her all night long until morning. They let her go at dawn.
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (the Levite) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “and he caused [her] to go outside to them.”
Heb “knew,” in the sexual sense.
verses.commentary:
19:25 "the man seized his concubine" There were no more love words (cf. Jdgs. 19:3)! He sacrificed her
for his own life. I am surprised this Levite did not offer his male servant to the homosexual mob. Apparently servants
were valued more than concubines.

Notice the actions of this sex-crazed mob.

- they raped her ‒ BDB 393, KB 390, Qal IMPERFECT with waw; this is literally
"knew," cf. Gen. 4:1

- they abused her ‒ BDB 759 I, KB 834, Hithpael IMPERFECT with waw,
cf. 1 Sam. 31:4; Jer. 38:19

- all night until morning ‒ repeated abuse which caused her death (Jdgs. 19:28)

Number 3 shows the prolonged attack by the mob. I must admit this account bothers me! This was a
horrible night for this poor woman. I feel the same sinking feeling about Job's family and servants (i.e., Job 1-2).
Remember, the Bible records what it does not advocate. In historical narratives one must look for the overall purpose
(i.e., Judges 17-21) and not focus on the details of the accounts.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

SPECIAL TOPIC: GENRE AND INTERPRETATION: OLD TESTAMENT NARRATIVES

verses.zh: 天快亮的时候，妇人回到她主人住宿的房门前，就仆倒在地，直到天亮。
verses.en: The woman arrived back at daybreak and was sprawled out on the doorstep of the house where her master[NOTE:1] was staying until it became light.[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew term here translated “master,” is plural. The plural indicates degree here and emphasizes the Levite’s absolute sovereignty over the woman.
Heb “The woman came at the turning of the morning and fell at the door of the house of the man where her master was until the light.”

verses.zh: 早晨，她的主人起来开了房门，出去要行路，不料那妇人仆倒在房门前，两手搭在门槛上；
verses.en: When her master[NOTE:1] got up in the morning, opened the doors of the house, and went outside to start on his journey, there was the woman, his concubine, sprawled out on the doorstep of the house with her hands on the threshold.
notes: The Hebrew term here translated “master,” is plural. The plural indicates degree here and emphasizes the Levite’s absolute sovereignty over the woman.
verses.commentary:
19:27-29 These verses show

- the Levite's callused feelings toward his concubine (as did his actions in Jdgs. 19:25)

- the Levite's anger and sense of violation expressed toward the whole tribe of Benjamin (Jdgs. 19:29)

The actions of

- the townspeople of Gibeah (i.e., no offer of shelter)

- the worthless fellows (i.e., sexual demands)

- the Levite (i.e., putting his concubine at the door for the mob and his callous reaction to her murder)

- the tribe of Benjamin (i.e., not punishing the worthless fellows in their midst)

- the over reaction of the Israeli tribes in destroying a whole tribe (i.e., men, women, and children)

This is the theological point of Judges 17-21. The editor/compiler thinks a righteous king would/could solve
the problem (cf. Jdgs. 19:1).

verses.zh: 就对妇人说：「起来，我们走吧！」妇人却不回答。那人便将她驮在驴上，起身回本处去了。
verses.en: He said to her, “Get up, let’s leave.” But there was no response. He put her on the donkey and went home.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “And the man took her on the donkey and arose and went to his place.”

verses.en: When he got home, he took a knife, grasped his concubine, and carved her up into twelve pieces.[NOTE:1] Then he sent the pieces throughout Israel.[NOTE:2]

verses.commentary:
19:29 "cut her in twelve pieces" This VERB is often used of sacrificial acts (BDB 677,
KB 732, cf. Exod. 29:17; Lev. 1:6, 12; 8:20). A similar act was performed by Saul to call the Twelve Tribes into
action (cf. 1 Sam. 11:7). In this case, Benjamin tried to protect these vile men of their tribe! Why, is not stated.

verses.en: Everyone who saw the sight[NOTE:1] said, “Nothing like this has happened or been witnessed during the entire time since[NOTE:2] the Israelites left the land of Egypt![NOTE:3] Take careful note of it! Discuss it and speak!”
notes: The words “the sight” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

BACKGROUND

- The central figure of Judges 17-18 is a Levite from Bethlehem, traveling in the hill country of Ephraim; strangely the
same type of person is also the object of Judges 19.

- The chronological order of Judges 19-21 does not follow 17-18, but appears to be very early in the period of the Judges.

- The purpose of this section is to show the moral and legal problems involved when there is no central, strong, godly
leadership. The horror of this crime is matched only by the over reaction of the tribes.

- Josephus, Antiq. 7.2.8, changes the story in several ways (i.e., traditions passed on to him).

- the lady was a very beautiful wife

- the men of Gibeah saw his wife and wanted her; this is different from the MT, which asserts clearly the homosexual
nature of the event

- the woman felt her Levite husband would not forgive her and would feel great shame, so she voluntarily died

This shows how Jewish tradition tried to spare the Levite the shame he so deserved!

- This account has similarity to Genesis 19 and 1 Samuel 11:7. Some think it is a merging of two different accounts.
I am very uncomfortable with the J.E.P.D. mentality. Moderns do not know the time, process, or date of how the OT
books reached their final form. Believers accept, by faith, that the Spirit guided the process. We cannot superimpose
modern textual criticism onto ancient ANE texts.

1Now it came about in those days, when there was no king in Israel, that there was a certain
Levite staying in the remote part of the hill country of Ephraim, who took a concubine for himself
from Bethlehem in Judah. 2But his concubine played the harlot against him, and she went away from
him to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah, and was there for a period of four months. 3Then
her husband arose and went after her to speak tenderly to her in order to bring her back, taking with
him his servant and a pair of donkeys. So she brought him into her father's house, and when the
girl's father saw him, he was glad to meet him. 4His father-in-law, the girl's father, detained him; and
he remained with him three days. So they ate and drank and lodged there. 5Now on the fourth day
they got up early in the morning, and he prepared to go; and the girl's father said to his son-in-law,
"Sustain yourself with a piece of bread, and afterward you may go." 6So both of them sat down and
ate and drank together; and the girl's father said to the man, "Please be willing to spend the night,
and let your heart be merry." 7Then the man arose to go, but his father-in-law urged him so that he
spent the night there again. 8On the fifth day he arose to go early in the morning, and the girl's father
said, "Please sustain yourself, and wait until afternoon"; so both of them ate. 9When the man arose
to go along with his concubine and servant, his father-in-law, the girl's father, said to him, "Behold
now, the day has drawn to a close; please spend the night. Lo, the day is coming to an end; spend the
night here that your heart may be merry. Then tomorrow you may arise early for your journey so
that you may go home."
